If anyone wants to participate, feel free to use my ideas if you mention me:

  • Make it possible/easier to turn off css. With slow internet, a large css file can break the experience completely. CSS-free pages should still be readable - reduce unnecessary large standard spacing after paragraphs and other such hindrances, make it easier to program pages which look fine w/ and w/o css in the next iteration of html. Create an accessibility badge which goes only to web pages which can easily be used on devices for the blind, on bad internet connections, and so on, and are readable in either case.

  • Make it possible/easier to turn off refresh. Manual refresh instead of automatically loading a new version when you hit the back button or browse your history would make so many things so much easier - especially when you have a bad internet connection. You should be able to search your browsing history and easily find things you looked up a week earlier, even if you don't have internet at the moment, and without saving everything. Even interactive items (like Google Maps or email) should open, and just show the parts you opened before. If you try to scroll to something which is not in the cache, it may be necessary to do a manual refresh before you can download missing parts. Even then, by hitting back or going through the browser, it should be possible to see the older stuff, though navigating might be more complex to avoid issues with data formats changing in the meantime. Going back to something should automatically make it last longer in the cache, and browsing history should also bring a button to keep the information from getting deleted when the cache gets full and create a link to it. When you open a page while you have internet, but it takes a long time to load, it would be nice to see the old version (with a clearly visible remark from when it is and how far the download of the new version is) until the new one is ready to be displayed. It should be possible to exclude pages from staying cached - like your banking. And there needs to be some thought to avoid accidental purchases and such.

  • Create a low-bandwidth mode which blocks bandwidth hoggers, w/o installing an ad-blocker. Videos and other animations/media should only download when you click on them, flashy advertisement should be possible to completely eliminate, and so on. Unlike an ad-blocker, the advertisers should have the option to replace the ad with low-bandwidth text/html content. They should also be able to provide lower quality/resolution images, videos, and so on, ideally following some standards to chose what would usually be determined from screen resolution and such.

  • Create standards for webmail, maps and other such interactive databases to store (some) content offline, like a classical email app. A change of data formats should ideally not matter. For instance, if an email in a webmailer had a tag marking it as such, including the format version, the page could be stored in the cache, and a database could hold according references. Changing the format would just change the old references, so that the older emails display fine in a current version of the webmailer, even if offline and some parts maybe looking slightly outdated.

  • Encrypt the keys for SSL so that some types of information can be stored in caches/proxies and opened on multiple computers, and the content provider still gets informed and keeps control who uses the data (and under which conditions, like advertisement to pay for the service, proxy providers sticking to privacy standards, or data being specific to an account). Maps for instance could be cached on multiple levels from regional servers to internet providers to local connection points to more intelligent routers, so that someone who looks up a map on his wifi-connected mobile phone and then opens the same map on his computer connected to the same router will only affect the router cache twice. Opening it on a mobile phone of the wife in the network of the same provider might get the third copy from a connection point. And so on. This would really save bandwidth on live transmissions of popular events - or when everyone tries to get the news during a catastrophic event, one of the goals of this competition - all without compromising privacy too much (though some info can be read from the fact that the cache is used, and a good guess would be verifiable through getting the data from the cache).

  • Wifi routers can usually open several channels. They should be able to connect to another router to get information if their own connection is bad. For instance, if a provider has routers in two neighboring countries, one with good access, one with bad access, they should be able to use the routers of customers close to the border to help the routers of customer on the other side of the borders. And those routers should be usable by routers a little further away. And so on. Customers sharing their connection may get benefits like being able to use their wifi wherever they are, as long as another shared router is near, to offset the slightly increased power bills. Further benefits may be added if people put an ethernet cable between routers in areas with bad and good coverage (which would also require some switching abilities in the routers, and maybe some legal work, like registering cross-border connections with authorities).

  • Phones might also be programmed to act as a relay when connected to power, not too hot, and in an area with not too much wifi congestion. They can already create hotspots with a few devices, so relaying should also work. Relay work may get internet points for the owners, so they profit from letting it happen, which helps poorer people get some internet, too. This opens up a whole box of other possibilities - like using 3g, 4g, lte, and so on to connect one phone (with enough battery charge), and then wifi, bluetooth, and such for surrounding phones, to improve coverage, reduce congestion, and get rid of blind spots. All automatically and w/o users realising it - except by reduced battery consumption for the majority and better reception for all.

  • Offer low capacity internet backbones at such low prices that anyone even in a developing country can easily become an isp. The backbones could be available through satellites, stationary blimps, directed radio antennas, and traditional cables. People would easily be able to increase capacity as needed. Ready made cheap servers would automatically chose between different backbones for redundancy, cache http pages and such, relay to each other, spread out dns services, and so on. Sponsored (advertisement financed) content (like soccer championships) and such might help subsidise them. The kicker: adding cables to connect to other nearby servers increases capacity and redundancy for free, thus giving incentive for locals to improve infrastructure w/o big company or government help. Universities and such might get a server for free, so that more content is ready to be used at maximum speed.

  • Create a cheap car radio which gets its music through the internet, too - besides acting as an internet relay and wifi router, so that one radio connected to a public wifi or a phone used as hotspot is able to provide internet to many surrounding cars, so that surrounding cars give redundancy for cars in areas with bad reception, and so on. A more advanced model may include satellite internet, built-in 3g/4g/lte (maybe even a phone relay), a navigation system, gps, and so on. Often heard music and other often used info may be cached in the radio, too.

  • Another place to market cheap internet relays as above maybe solar power stations: Sell a solar panel with a small router (connected to the internet through any available means), some usb power outlets to charge a few phones or so, with the option to add a battery for power at night. If a phone internet connection is locked to a provider, they may subsidise it a little. The best thing is: Someone who pays for his internet would get it even if the local 3g/4g/lte is not available, if there's an indirect connection to a nearby other cell phone tower. Also, they might be programmed to help distribute data traffic to where it is less congested.
